Physics · Gravitation · Cosmology

Rohan Bolle

Physics researcher in gravitation, cosmology, and computational modeling

I earned my B.S. in Physics and Astronomy from Georgia Southern University in May 2026, with a minor in Mathematics. My undergraduate research with Dr. Jeffery Secrest focuses on cosmological models in which the gravitational parameter varies with the scale factor of the universe.

My work combines analytical derivations with numerical modeling in Python. I have studied modified Friedmann dynamics, gravitational phase transitions, quantum-cosmological corrections, and parameter regimes that produce qualitatively different early-universe behavior.

I am especially interested in extending this background toward gravitational-wave astrophysics and broader problems in gravitation where analytical physics and computation meet.

Current & Published Work

Research

Analytical and computational work in modified gravity, cosmology, and deformed mathematical frameworks.

Current project · Georgia Southern University · Manuscript in preparation

Scale-Dependent Gravity in Quantum Cosmology I

My current research explores cosmological models in which the gravitational parameter varies with the scale factor, G(a), allowing gravity to evolve between different regimes in the early universe. I work on both the analytical formulation and Python-based numerical modeling, using the resulting solutions to study how a changing gravitational coupling affects expansion, phase transitions, recollapse, and singularity-related behavior.

Research focus
  • Modified Friedmann dynamics with G(a).
  • Numerical evolution and parameter-space exploration.
  • Gravitational phase transitions and recollapse scenarios.
  • Wheeler-DeWitt dynamics, singularity avoidance, and semiclassical recovery.
Modified Gravity Quantum Cosmology Friedmann Dynamics Python Numerical Modeling
Published 2025 · Mathematical and Computational Applications 30(5), 115

An Exposition on the Kaniadakis κ-Deformed Decay Differential Equation

This project examined a first-order decay equation within the Kaniadakis κ-deformed framework. I contributed to the analytical and numerical study of the modified decay law, focusing on how the deformation parameter changes the solution relative to the ordinary exponential case and how the formalism connects to broader applications in non-extensive statistical mechanics.

Conference Work

Talks & Posters

Selected presentations tracing the development of my work on scale-dependent gravity and early-universe cosmology.

Oral GS4 Symposium · Georgia Southern University, Statesboro Campus · 2026

Gravitational Phase Transitions in Cosmological Models with a Scale-Factor-Dependent Gravitational Constant

Presented the central idea of the scale-dependent-gravity model and showed how allowing G to vary with the cosmological scale factor changes the evolution of the universe. The talk connected the analytical setup of the model with numerical solutions and the physical interpretation of the resulting cosmological behavior.

Oral GS4 Symposium · Georgia Southern University, Armstrong Campus · 2026

Scale-Dependent Gravity and Early-Universe Dynamics: Exploring Cosmological Phase Transitions

A second oral presentation of the same research program, framed around the evolution of the model across different gravitational regimes. This version emphasized the numerical behavior of the cosmological solutions, the role of the model parameters, and the broader physical questions raised by a scale-dependent gravitational coupling.

Poster Southeastern Section of the American Physical Society · Oxford, MS · November 2022

Gravitational Phase Transition in the Early Universe

This poster represents an earlier stage of the project and introduced the idea of modeling an evolving gravitational parameter in the early universe. It presented the motivation for the model together with preliminary mathematical and numerical results that later developed into the broader scale-dependent-gravity research program.
